hints: Draw out D as $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH(CH}_3)_2$ and find the longest chain containing the $\text{C=C}$ bond, then number from the end closest to the double bond.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain and number it**
Look at D in Fig. 4.1. The longest chain through the double bond has 4 carbons, so it is a butene. Number from the right so the $\text{C=C}$ starts at carbon 1, giving $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-$ as C1-C2. The methyl branch is then on C3, so the name is 3-methylbut-1-ene.

hints: Recall the two conditions for cis/trans isomerism: restricted rotation about $\text{C=C}$ and two different groups on each carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Check what is attached to each end of the double bond**
For cis/trans to exist you need two different groups on the left C and two different groups on the right C. In C, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3$, the left carbon has two $\text{CH}_3$ groups. In D, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}=\text{CH}_2$, the right carbon has two H atoms. With identical groups on one end, swapping positions gives the same structure, so no geometrical isomers exist.
Final answer: Both C and D have one carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ bond attached to two identical groups, so cis/trans isomerism is not possible.

hints: A positional isomer keeps the same skeleton and formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ but moves the position of the $\text{C=C}$ bond to a different place.
walkthrough:
Move the double bond, keep the atoms**
C is 2-methylbut-2-ene and D is 3-methylbut-1-ene. Both are $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$. Keep five carbons with one methyl branch but put the $\text{C=C}$ in a new position. A neat choice is $\text{CH}_2=\text{C(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The double bond is now at C1 on a 2-methyl chain, so it is positional isomerism, not chain or functional group isomerism.
Final answer: 2-methylbut-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{C(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ shown as skeletal structure.

hints: Remember that $\text{H}_2$ with Pt adds two H atoms across the $\text{C=C}$ bond to give the saturated alkane with the same carbon skeleton.
walkthrough:
Saturate the double bond**
D is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}=\text{CH}_2$. Hydrogenation simply adds one H to each C of the $\text{C=C}$. The skeleton does not change, so you get $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is 2-methylbutane.
Final answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (2-methylbutane)

hints: Picture the $\text{C=C}$ of C opening to a single bond, with the two carbons linking to neighbours on both sides to form the backbone.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond into a repeat unit**
C is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH(CH}_3)$. In addition polymerisation the pi bond breaks and each alkene carbon forms two new single bonds along the chain. So the left C keeps its two $\text{CH}_3$ groups and the right C keeps its $\text{CH}_3$ and H. Draw $-\text{C(CH}_3)_2-\text{CH(CH}_3)-$ with extension bonds on each backbone C to show it repeats.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $-\text{C(CH}_3)_2-\text{CH(CH}_3)-$ with continuation bonds through the backbone carbons.

hints: Recall that the ratio of [M+1] to [M] intensities is approximately $1.1\%$ per carbon atom, so set up $(2.7/48.7) \times 100$ divided by $1.1$.
Check the $M_r$ from $m/e = 70$ against the $M_r$ of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ calculated from $5 \times 12 + 10 \times 1$.
walkthrough:
Use the M+1 intensity to count carbons**
The small M+1 peak is almost entirely due to $^{13}\text{C}$. Each carbon contributes about $1.1\%$ of the M intensity to M+1. So:
$$ \text{number of C} = \frac{\text{intensity M+1}}{\text{intensity M}} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = \frac{2.7}{48.7} \times \frac{100}{1.1} \approx 5.04 $$
That rounds to 5 carbons.

Match the mass**
For $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$:
$$ M_r = 5 \times 12 + 10 \times 1 = 70 $$
This exactly matches the molecular ion at $m/e = 70$, so the data is consistent with $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$.

Final answer: Number of C $= \frac{2.7}{48.7} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 5.04 \approx 5$
$M_r$ of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} = 5(12) + 10(1) = 70$, matching $m/e = 70$, consistent.

hints: Start by polarising $\text{H-Br}$ as $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ and think about which species the electron rich $\text{C=C}$ will attack.
Consider which of the two possible carbocations from C is more substituted and therefore forms in the first step.
Remember the second step is attack of $\text{Br}^-$ with a lone pair on the positively charged carbon.
walkthrough:
Show the first attack on H**
$\text{HBr}$ is polar: $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ because Br is more electronegative. The $\text{C=C}$ is electron rich, so draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=C}$ bond to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$, and a curly arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond onto Br to give $\text{Br}^-$. The H adds to the $\text{CH}$ end of C so the positive charge lands on the more substituted carbon.

Draw the Markovnikov intermediate**
Adding H to $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3$ at the right hand carbon gives $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, a tertiary carbocation. This is the major intermediate because it is stabilised by three alkyl groups.

Capture the carbocation with bromide**
Now draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ to the $\text{C}^+$. This forms the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and gives E, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(Br)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ as shown in Fig. 4.2.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$, curly arrow $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$, curly arrow $\text{H-Br}$ to $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ to give tertiary carbocation $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
Step 2: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{C}^+$ to give E, 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

hints: Apply Markovnikov's rule to D, $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}=\text{CH}_2$: H adds to the carbon with more H atoms, Br ends up on the more substituted carbon.
walkthrough:
Place Br on the more substituted carbon**
For D, H from HBr adds to the terminal $\text{CH}_2$ to give the more stable secondary carbocation, then $\text{Br}^-$ bonds to C2. The product is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH(Br)CH}_3$. C2 is attached to H, Br, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$, four different groups, so it is chiral as required for F.
Final answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH(Br)CH}_3$ (2-bromo-3-methylbutane), containing a chiral centre at C2.

hints: List the two possible carbocations that can form from each alkene and label them primary, secondary or tertiary.
Recall how alkyl groups donate electron density by the positive inductive effect to stabilise a neighbouring $\text{C}^+$.
walkthrough:
Compare the possible intermediates**
Sit beside the two structures. Protonation of C gives a choice of tertiary $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ or secondary carbocation. Protonation of D gives a choice of secondary or primary carbocation. The reaction goes via the most stable one in each case.

Link alkyl groups to stability**
Alkyl groups push electron density toward the $\text{C}^+$ by the positive inductive effect, spreading the charge and lowering energy. More alkyl groups means greater stabilisation: tertiary is more stable than secondary, which is more stable than primary. So C reacts via its tertiary cation while D can only reach a secondary cation, leading to different Markovnikov products E and F.

Final answer: C can form tertiary and secondary carbocations, D can form secondary and primary carbocations.
Alkyl groups have a positive inductive (+I) effect, more alkyl groups give a more stable carbocation. The tertiary carbocation from C is more stable than the secondary from D, so different major products form.

hints: Identify reaction 2 as conversion of tertiary bromoalkane E to a tertiary alcohol J, think of aqueous hydrolysis conditions.
Identify reaction 3 as vigorous oxidative cleavage of alkene C to two carbonyls, one of which is propanone, think of hot concentrated oxidiser.
Identify reaction 4 as formation of ester H from alcohol J plus carboxylic acid G, think of the acid catalyst used for esterification.
walkthrough:
Work out E to J**
E is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane and J must be the corresponding tertiary alcohol $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ to later make the ester H. Bromoalkane to alcohol is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{OH}^-$, so use $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, usually warmed. Aqueous is essential, ethanolic would give elimination.

Work out C to G plus propanone**
Reaction 3 splits the $\text{C=C}$ of C into two carbonyl fragments. One fragment is propanone $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{O}$, the other G must be ethanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. This vigorous cleavage needs hot, acidified, concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$. Cold dilute $\text{KMnO}_4$ would only give a diol.

Work out J plus G to ester H**
H is an ethanoate ester of the tertiary alcohol J. Carboxylic acid plus alcohol to ester is esterification, which needs a few drops of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst with warming. This completes the route: $\text{J} + \text{G} \rightarrow \text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Final answer: Reaction 2: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ (aqueous sodium hydroxide, heat)
Reaction 3: hot, acidified, concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$
Reaction 4: conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst (warm)
